links.note: In 1862 Pius IX and Ecuador signed a pact in Rome that kept the state's faith Catholic. It tied every school to church teaching and let bishops alone pick the books for religion. In 1895 Mexico's Guadalupe image was to be crowned in the name of Pope Leo XIII and by his order, part of a pull toward Rome that historians call "Romanization."

major.reason: Article 3 of a concordat made by the pope and the republic sets rules by authority: all teaching shall conform to Catholic doctrine, and bishops alone shall choose the books for religion and morals. Article 1 only continues ('esse perget') the existing state religion, so the call no longer rests on it.

links.outcome: In 1862 Pope Pius IX and Ecuador agreed that every school would follow Catholic teaching. Only bishops would choose the books used to teach religion.
wants: Acta et decreta Concilii Plenarii Americae Latinae (Rome, 1899/1900): the 1899 council the text names
Papal letters on recognition of the new republics' bishops (Leo XII, Gregory XVI), for 'Rome's slow recognition'
drafter_flags: Round 1: article 1 says Catholicism 'esse perget', shall continue to be, the state religion. The note now says 'kept', and the major call rests on article 3 (lines 25590-25594), which lays down new school and textbook rules in the future tense. The concordat's text does not say what rule stood before it; the call rests on its being a settlement fixed by the two authorities.
Article 3 also gives bishops the right to ban books and binds the government to keep such books out (lines 25594-25599). The outcome keeps to the school and textbook clauses.
Mirbt notes the concordat was set aside on 28 June 1878 (lines 25581-25582); neither note nor outcome claims it lasted.

The Guadalupe patronage decree in the prologue (lines 220-222) is undated, and the editors' note (lines 8722-8724) dates the confirmation of the patronage to Benedict XIV in 1754, which is colonial. It is dropped. The note now uses the dated Roman act of this period: Leo XIII's grant of the coronation, set for 12 October 1895 (lines 8725-8727), done 'in the name of the Supreme Pontiff and by his order' (lines 251-253).
'Rome (Holy See)' is matched to the long-nineteenth-century Catholic entry, as for Haiti and the Chaldean recognition.
Serbin 2006 is repo-cited for Brazil's 'Romanizing bishops'; not rechecked.
links.change_reason: Round 2 finding 1, applied as written: the 1895 date belongs to the coronation, not to the papal order.

links.note: A list of the Coptic patriarchs of Alexandria, printed by E. A. Wallis Budge in 1928, runs as one numbered line from the 1300s to 1854. It counts the reformer who took office in 1854 as the 110th, naming him Cyril V, though most lists call him Cyril IV. No other Coptic stage is set out between 1300 and 1854, so this line spans five centuries and rests on modern lists.

drafter_flags: Round 1 (finding 4): Budge's 1928 table is an editor's compilation, so it is now listed as a secondary (with its file, lines and a verbatim quote, as the Conybeare source on the Old Believers link is) and the grade is Dominant Modern Reconstruction. No vendored original witness was found for the see across 1300-1854: Quatremère 1811 quotes al-Maqrizi on single fifteenth-century successions only (e.g. lines 9703-9707), and its year for the death of Matthew does not match Budge's table, so it is not cited.
The type's test, continuity of the same see, is what Budge's numbered line shows: entries 85 to 110 run without a missing number, though OCR garbles nos. 99-101 (lines 2843-2845).
Lead's guidance: kept without waiting for a ruling, and the missing middle Coptic movement is escalated as a map gap. The note says plainly that no Coptic stage stands between.
OCR reads '109' as 'tog'; the quote keeps the OCR exactly.
Budge names the 1854-1861 patriarch 'Cyril V'; most modern lists, and this movement's own text, call him Cyril IV. The note says so.
